newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Court challenge to Manila ban on Nobel laureate.
newsitem.headline: Court challenge to Manila ban on Nobel laureate.

text.p: Philippine human rights groups petitioned the Supreme Court on Thursday to lift a ban on Nobel Peace Prize winner Jose Ramos-Horta, arguing it violated their rights to freedom of information.

"The government has not given any valid or satisfactory reason to deny his application for a visa," the Manila People's Forum, a coalition of non-government organisations (NGOs), said in its 29-page petition to the court.

The Forum had invited East Timor resistance campaigner Ramos-Horta to an international NGO meeting to be held in parallel with the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum summit being hosted by the Philippines from November 22-25.

The petition, which named Foreign Affairs Secretary Domingo Siazon and Immigration Commissioner Edgar Mendoza, said the Philippine ban on Ramos-Horta's entry violated the NGOs' rights to hear and form their own opinion about his views.
"The violation of the petitioners' right to information and freedom of thought, opinion, speech, expression and assembly is...unjustified and unconstitutional," the petition said.
Manila banned Ramos-Horta after he accepted an invitation to address the international NGO conference on November 21-23, saying his presence could disrupt the APEC meeting.

But the NGOs said the government was not able to explain how the presence of Ramos-Horta would expose President Fidel Ramos to embarrassment and possible disturbances in the country, or prevent a successful and productive meeting of the APEC leaders.
One of the leaders expected to attend the November 25 summit is Indonesian President Suharto.
Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975 and annexed it the next year in a move never accepted by the United Nations.
Ramos-Horta, who lives in exile in Sydney, was denied a visa on October 24 when he applied at the Philippine consulate there.
The NGOs said the denial of Ramos-Horta's visa application was "arbitrary".
"Ramos-Horta need not even have applied for a visa, as temporary visitors are allowed an initial stay of 22 days without a visa," the NGOs said.
"However, Ramos-Horta, in good faith, in respect for Philippine laws, and the government's pronouncements that he may not be allowed into the country, did apply for a visa," they added.
The Philippines stood to lose its reputation as a bastion of democracy if it denied entry to Ramos-Horta, the NGOs said.
"The Philippines would be known as a country which would violate human rights in the face of pressure from its neighbours," they said.
The Philippines barred Ramos-Horta and other East Timorese dissidents from entering the country in 1994 during an international human rights conference on East Timor.
